etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English simplicite, from Old French simplicite, from Latin simplicitās, from simplex (“simple”). See simple. Partially displaced native English onefoldness.

definitions.definition: The quality or state of being unmixed or uncompounded
The quality or state of being not complex, or of consisting of few parts.

quote.citation: 1951 July, “British Standard Locomotives”, in Railway Magazine, pages 438-439:
quote.text: 2. Simplicity, with the least number of working parts, all readily visible and accessible.

definitions.definition: Lack of sharpness of mind; lack of ability to think using complex ideas; stupidity
Lack of artificial ornament, pretentious style, or luxury; plainness
Lack of subtlety or abstruseness; clarity

quote.citation: 2013 August 3, “Boundary problems”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8847:
quote.text: Economics is a messy discipline: too fluid to be a science, too rigorous to be an art. Perhaps it is fitting that economists’ most-used metric, gross domestic product (GDP), is a tangle too. GDP measures the total value of output in an economic territory. Its apparent simplicity explains why it is scrutinised down to tenths of a percentage point every month.

definitions.definition: The state or quality of being simple
(archaic, rare) An act or instance of foolishness.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 31, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: speaking of the great simplicity we commit, in leaving yong children under the government and charge of their fathers and parents.
